title.en: Central nervous system examination in children

intro.en: Bedside testing of a child with a suspected nerve or muscle disorder, from history and higher functions through cranial nerves, motor, sensory, reflex, cerebellar and meningeal signs.

items.summary: A focused history that covers development, limb weakness, feeling changes, cranial nerve clues, fits and raised pressure signs.

blocks.title: Developmental history
bullets: Record gross motor, fine motor, personal social, language, vision and hearing milestones in order.
Note any halt or loss of skills already gained, with the age it began.

blocks.title: Weakness or tightness
bullets: Ask duration, mode of onset and whether it is static, improving or worsening.
Distal hand trouble shows as fumbling with buttons or a loose shoe grip.
Proximal leg and shoulder trouble shows as hard combing, bathing or rising from a squat.
List linked complaints such as pain, cramps, falls or bladder change.

blocks.title: Sensory and bowel bladder clues
bullets: Ask about numbness, burning or altered touch, heat and cold sense.
Ask about constipation, retention, incontinence and urgency.

blocks.title: Cranial nerve clues
bullets: Smell loss or change; blurring, field cuts or double vision.
Feeding trouble, dribbling, food leaking, mouth pulled to a side, weak eye closure, lost taste.
Hearing loss or ringing; nasal voice, fluid escaping through the nose.
Weak shoulder shrug; slurred speech or trouble swallowing.

blocks.title: Fits, balance and pressure signs
bullets: For fits record type, onset, length, course, continence during events and the recovery phase.
For balance ask about swaying, veering while walking and clumsy hand to mouth reach.
Ask about headache, vomiting, blurred vision, fever and altered alertness.

viva.q: How do you separate proximal from distal weakness in history?
viva.a: Proximal weakness limits combing, bathing and rising from a squat. Distal weakness limits buttoning and gripping footwear.

viva.q: What fit details must you always record?
viva.a: Type, onset, duration, course, bowel bladder control during the fit and the postictal state.

viva.q: Which history points suggest raised intracranial pressure?
viva.a: Headache, vomiting, blurring of vision and altered sensorium, with or without fever.

items.summary: A brief whole child survey followed by a clear account of how the child lies or sits, including stiff postures.

blocks.title: Steps
bullets: Do a full general survey first: vitals, growth, dysmorphism, skin, anaemia and systemic signs.
Then watch the resting pose of trunk and limbs without disturbing the child.
Name abnormal flexion or extension attitudes and any asymmetry between sides.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Describe the posture before touching the child, since handling changes tone.
Decorticate rigidity means flexed arms with extended legs and points to injury above the midbrain.
Record whether the pose is held all the time or appears only on stimulation.

viva.q: Why describe posture before the rest of the motor examination?
viva.a: Handling alters tone and pose, so the resting attitude must be captured first for accuracy.

viva.q: What is decorticate rigidity?
viva.a: Flexion of the upper limbs with extension of the lower limbs, seen with lesions above the midbrain.

items.summary: Testing of alertness, orientation, memory, intellect, thought, speech and sleep in an age appropriate way.

blocks.title: Steps
bullets: Grade alertness from full wakefulness through drowsy, stupor and obtundation to light coma, deep coma and flaccid coma.
Check orientation to time, place and person using questions the age group can answer.
Test immediate, recent and remote recall with suitable everyday events.

blocks.title: Thought, speech and sleep
bullets: Judge intellect against expected school and play performance for age.
Ask about false perceptions and fixed false beliefs, and note delirium.
Classify speech as normal, dysphasic, aphasic or dysarthric.
Ask the caregiver about usual sleep pattern and recent change.

viva.q: How do you record level of consciousness in words?
viva.a: Alert, drowsy, stupor, obtundation, delirium, then light, deep and flaccid coma in worsening order.

viva.q: What three parts of memory do you test?
viva.a: Immediate, recent and remote memory, using age appropriate everyday events.

viva.q: How do you describe abnormal speech at the bedside?
viva.a: Dysphasia is faulty language content, aphasia is loss of language, dysarthria is faulty articulation.

items.summary: Bedside smell testing of each nostril in turn with a familiar non irritant odour.

blocks.title: Steps
bullets: Confirm the nasal passage is open and free of blockage before testing.
Ask the child to shut the eyes while you close one nostril.
Offer a mild familiar scent such as coffee powder to each side separately.
Ask the child to name or point out the smell for each nostril.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Never use a sharp vapour such as ammonia because it stimulates pain fibres, not smell.
The first, second and eighth nerves carry only sensory fibres.

blocks.title: Nerve fibre types
blocks.text: Nerves one, two and eight are sensory only; five, nine and ten carry both motor and sensory fibres, and all the rest are motor only.

viva.q: How do you test smell in a child?
viva.a: Check the nose is clear, close the eyes and one nostril, then offer coffee powder to each side in turn.

viva.q: Why must ammonia never be used for smell testing?
viva.a: It is pungent and stimulates trigeminal pain endings rather than the olfactory nerve.

items.summary: Checking of sharpness, fields, colour, light reflexes and the optic fundus in a child.

blocks.title: Acuity of vision
bullets: Test distant sharpness with a Snellen chart and near sharpness with a Jaeger chart.
When charts are not possible use finger counting, hand movement and light perception.
Snellen rows are read at 60, 36, 24, 18, 12, 9, 6 and 5 metres.
Acuity equals the test distance divided by the row distance; full vision is 6/6.

blocks.title: Fields, colour and fundus
bullets: Map fields by formal perimetry after 7 years or by confrontation after 3 years, seated about 3 feet away.
Test colour sense with Ishihara plates after 3 years of age.
Inspect the fundus and check pupillary light and accommodation reflexes.

viva.q: What does 6/6 vision mean?
viva.a: The child reads at 6 metres what should be read at 6 metres, which is normal acuity.

viva.q: How do field tests differ with age?
viva.a: Confrontation from 3 years, formal perimetry from 7 years, at about 3 feet distance.

viva.q: Which charts test near and distant vision?
viva.a: Jaeger chart for near vision and Snellen chart for distant vision.

title.en: Third, fourth and sixth nerves: eye movements

items.summary: Study of lids, alignment and gaze in every direction with pupil reflexes.

blocks.title: Steps
bullets: Keep the head straight and neutral before asking for any eye movement.
Look for drooping lids, jerky eyes and squint, using a cover uncover test.
Move a target through each gaze direction and watch range and symmetry.
Check pupil size, shape, direct and consensual light response and accommodation.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: The lateral rectus is supplied by the sixth nerve and the superior oblique by the fourth.
Note nystagmus, ptosis and strabismus by name since they localise the fault.

viva.q: Which muscles do the fourth and sixth nerves supply?
viva.a: The fourth supplies superior oblique and the sixth supplies lateral rectus, recalled as SO4 and LR6.

viva.q: What do you check in the pupils?
viva.a: Size, shape, direct and consensual light reflexes and the accommodation response.

viva.q: How do you look for a squint?
viva.a: Inspect alignment and do a cover uncover test with the head held neutral.

items.summary: Testing of face feeling, chewing muscles and the corneal and jaw reflexes.

blocks.title: Inspection and sensory part
bullets: Look at the chewing muscles for hollowing or asymmetry.
Test touch across the forehead, cheek and jaw zones on both sides.
Map the ophthalmic, maxillary and mandibular territories separately.

blocks.title: Motor part
bullets: Feel masseter and temporalis bulk while the child clenches the teeth.
Ask for sideways jaw shifts to test the pterygoid muscles.
Ask the child to open the mouth against your hand to test the depressors.

blocks.title: Reflexes
bullets: Elicit the corneal reflex and the jaw jerk.
Loss of the corneal response points to the fifth or seventh nerve arc.

viva.q: Which muscles do you palpate for the trigeminal motor part?
viva.a: Masseter and temporalis on clenching, pterygoids on sideways shift and jaw openers against resistance.

viva.q: What are the two trigeminal reflexes?
viva.a: The corneal reflex and the jaw jerk.

viva.q: Which face zones map the three divisions?
viva.a: Forehead for ophthalmic, cheek for maxillary and jaw for mandibular.

items.summary: Testing of face movement, front tongue taste and tear and saliva flow.

blocks.title: History and look
bullets: Ask about mouth pulled to a side, food or saliva leaking and sound seeming too loud.
Watch the whole face at rest for flattening of folds and droop.

blocks.title: Sensory and secretomotor part
bullets: Test taste on the front two thirds of the tongue by pointing to words on a card.
Assess watering and salivation; Schirmer paper sits under the lower lid for a timed spell.

blocks.title: Motor part
bullets: Test brow lift and frown for frontalis, steadying the scalp with one hand.
Test tight eye closure for orbicularis oculi and watch for upward rolling of the eye.
Test tooth show for the corner depressors, cheek puffing for buccinator and neck strapping for platysma.
Note the fold beside the nose, lost on the weak side.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: A lesion above the nucleus spares the forehead, while a lower lesion weakens the whole half face.
Bell upward rolling of the eye appears when lid closure is weak.

unsure: Source gives conflicting Schirmer timing (removed after 5 min, normal marking after 10 min); exact timing left out.

viva.q: Which face muscles test each branch?
viva.a: Frontalis for brow, orbicularis oculi for closure, mouth corner muscles for grin, buccinator for puff, platysma for neck.

viva.q: How do upper and lower facial weakness differ?
viva.a: An upper lesion spares the forehead, a lower lesion weakens the whole half of the face.

viva.q: What is Bell phenomenon?
viva.a: The eyeball rolls upward when the child tries to close a weak eyelid.

title.en: Eighth cranial nerve: hearing and balance

items.summary: Bedside checks of giddiness and of hearing with voice, watch and tuning fork tests.

blocks.title: Vestibular part
bullets: Ask about spells of spinning, unsteadiness and vomiting with head movement.
Watch stance and gait for a vestibular cause of veering.

blocks.title: Cochlear part
bullets: Screen with whispered voice and a ticking watch near each ear.
Compare air and bone conduction with Rinne testing and lateralisation with Weber testing.
Use a 256 or 512 Hz fork for both fork tests.

viva.q: Which fork frequency do you use for Rinne and Weber?
viva.a: A 256 or 512 Hz tuning fork.

viva.q: What does the vestibular history ask?
viva.a: Spinning vertigo, unsteadiness and vomiting linked to head movement.

viva.q: What bedside screens come before the fork?
viva.a: Whispered voice and a ticking watch held near each ear.

title.en: Ninth and tenth nerves: palate, voice and swallow

items.summary: Testing of back tongue taste, palate lift, voice quality, swallow and the gag reflex.

blocks.title: Sensory part
bullets: Taste over the back third of the tongue belongs to the ninth nerve.
Ask about choking, cough on feeds and fluid returning through the nose.

blocks.title: Motor part
bullets: Listen for a nasal twang and slurred or hoarse speech.
Watch the soft palate rise and note which way the uvula points.
Test the gag response on each side and compare.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: The uvula swings away from a weak tenth nerve, toward the healthy side.
Both nerves are mixed motor and sensory in type.

viva.q: Where does ninth nerve taste come from?
viva.a: The posterior third of the tongue.

viva.q: Which way does the uvula move in a tenth nerve palsy?
viva.a: Away from the weak side, toward the healthy side.

viva.q: What feeding symptoms point to these nerves?
viva.a: Dysphagia, dysarthria, nasal regurgitation and a nasal voice.

title.en: Eleventh and twelfth nerves: shoulder, neck and tongue

items.summary: Testing of shrug and head turn strength plus tongue bulk, position and movement.

blocks.title: Eleventh nerve
bullets: Stand behind the child and test shoulder shrug for trapezius power.
Test head turning against your hand for sternocleidomastoid power.
Ask about prior trouble shrugging or rotating the neck.

blocks.title: Twelfth nerve
bullets: Ask about slurred speech before looking inside the mouth.
Note tongue bulk, wasting, twitching and resting lie.
Ask the child to push the tongue straight out and watch the direction.

blocks.title: Rule of 17 for deviation
bullets: Seven plus ten is seventeen: mouth and uvula both swing away from the weak side.
Five plus twelve is seventeen: jaw and tongue both swing toward the weak side.
The tongue points to the weak side and so tells the truth about the lesion.

viva.q: How do you test the eleventh nerve?
viva.a: Shrug against resistance for trapezius and head turning against resistance for sternocleidomastoid.

viva.q: State the rule of 17.
viva.a: Seventh and tenth palsies deviate away from the lesion; fifth and twelfth deviate toward it.

viva.q: Which way does a weak tongue point?
viva.a: Toward the weak side on protrusion.

credit.author: Mukherjee SK, Gowshami CB, Salam A, Kuddus R, Farazi MA, Baksh J

title.en: Motor system: limb attitude, bulk and tone

items.summary: Inspection of resting limb pose, measurement of muscle bulk and grading of resistance to passive movement.

blocks.title: Attitude and nutrition
bullets: Record the resting lie of upper and lower limbs separately.
Judge size, shape and side to side symmetry of each muscle group.
Tape mid arm, mid forearm, mid thigh and mid calf on both sides and compare.

blocks.title: Tone testing
bullets: Ask the child to relax fully and go floppy before you handle any limb.
Feel the muscle belly, then move each joint slowly through its range.
A limp floppy limb with excess range means low tone; a stiff held limb with cut range means high tone.
Name clasp knife release, uniform lead pipe stiffness and ratchety cogwheel stiffness.

blocks.title: Tone in the newborn
bullets: In a neonate use the scarf sign, heel to ear pull and hip adductor angle.
Interpret the angles against expected maturity for that age.

viva.q: How do you test tone?
viva.a: The child relaxes fully while you feel bulk, then move each joint passively and note resistance and range.

viva.q: How does low tone differ from high tone?
viva.a: Low tone is floppy with extra range; high tone is stiff with cut range and brisk resistance.

viva.q: Which three manoeuvres test newborn tone?
viva.a: Scarf sign, heel to ear manoeuvre and adductor angle.

title.en: Motor system: power grading and joint testing

items.summary: Zero to five strength grading applied joint by joint from neck to ankle, with trunk and breathing muscles.

head: Grade
Finding
rows: Faint tightening with no joint motion
Motion only when gravity is removed

blocks.title: Order of testing
bullets: Test neck bending forward and back, then shoulder lift, spread, closure and elevation.
Test elbow bend, straighten, palm up and palm down, then wrist bend and straighten.
Test finger grip by asking the child to squeeze two of your fingers.
Watch chest expansion and abdominal tightening; note splinting of ribs or diaphragm.
Test hip bend, straighten, spread, closure and inward and outward turn.
Test knee bend and straighten, then ankle pull up, push down, turn in and turn out.

blocks.title: Single muscle checks
bullets: Hands clasped behind the back tests latissimus dorsi.
Pushing at a wall with straight arms tests serratus anterior and shows winging if weak.
Clapping with arms forward tests pectoralis major.
Lifting the arm sideways from the chest tests deltoid and supraspinatus.
Straightening the bent elbow against your push tests triceps; holding the bend tests biceps.
Bending the half turned forearm tests brachioradialis.
Cocking the wrist back and forward against your grip tests wrist extensors and flexors.
For the thigh, straight leg lift tests psoas; pushing the spread leg inward tests adductors.
For hip turn, prone knee bent leg swings test inward and outward rotators.

viva.q: Recite the 0 to 5 power scale.
viva.a: 0 none, 1 flicker, 2 gravity removed, 3 against gravity, 4 against some resistance, 5 normal.

viva.q: How do you spot serratus anterior weakness?
viva.a: Pushing forward at a wall brings out medial winging of the scapula.

viva.q: What is Beevor sign territory?
viva.a: Abdominal wall weakness, tested with trunk flexion and umbilical shift.

items.summary: Finger nose and heel knee tests, a survey for extra movements and naming of the walking pattern.

blocks.title: Coordination
bullets: Do finger to nose testing in the arms and heel to knee testing in the legs.
Do each side alone and compare speed, wobble and overshoot.

blocks.title: Involuntary movements
bullets: Watch at rest and in action for fasciculation, tremor, chorea, athetosis and hemiballism.
Record site, rhythm, symmetry and what brings the movement out.

blocks.title: Gait
bullets: Label the walk as hemiparetic, ataxic, shuffling, high stepping, waddling or spastic.
Look for Gower sign: the child climbs up the legs with the hands to stand.
Gower sign points toward Duchenne muscular dystrophy.

viva.q: Which two tests check limb coordination?
viva.a: Finger nose test for the arms and heel knee test for the legs.

viva.q: What is Gower sign and what does it suggest?
viva.a: Climbing up the legs with the hands to stand, suggesting Duchenne muscular dystrophy.

viva.q: Name gait patterns you must recognise.
viva.a: Hemiparetic, ataxic, shuffling, high stepping, waddling and spastic.

items.summary: Side to side testing of touch, pain, temperature, back column senses and cortical senses with landmark dermatome levels.

blocks.title: How to test
bullets: Ask the child to close the eyes and answer aloud to each touch.
Test each skin segment on both sides and compare matched points.

blocks.title: Lateral column senses
bullets: Brush with cotton for light touch.
Use warm and cold water tubes for temperature.
Use a pin head for sharp pain.

blocks.title: Posterior column senses
bullets: Test crude touch and deep pressure.
Test buzz with a 128 Hz fork over bony points: inner ankle, shin bump, hip crest, wrist head, elbow, mastoid.
Test joint position sense in fingers and toes, plus overall limb position sense.
Do Romberg stance: sway with eyes shut points to back column loss.

blocks.title: Cortical senses
bullets: Test touch localisation, touch discrimination and two point discrimination with a compass.
Test stereognosis with known objects placed in the hand.
Test number tracing on skin (graphesthesia).
Check for sensory inattention and for dressing and construction apraxia.

blocks.title: Dermatome landmarks
bullets: Thumb maps to C6 and big toe to L4.
Nipple maps to T4 and umbilicus to T10.
Perianal skin maps to S3.

viva.q: What fork and sites test vibration?
viva.a: A 128 Hz fork on inner ankle, shin, hip crest, wrist, elbow and mastoid, both sides.

viva.q: Name three cortical sensory tests.
viva.a: Two point discrimination, stereognosis with objects and number tracing on skin.

viva.q: Give four dermatome landmarks.
viva.a: Thumb C6, nipple T4, umbilicus T10, big toe L4, perianal skin S3.

items.summary: Skin and mucosal reflexes with their root values, tendon jerks with roots and responses, plus grading and reinforcement.

head: Reflex
Root or arc
Note
rows: In by fifth nerve, out by seventh
Stroke toward the navel; lost in upper motor lesions
Stroke toward the navel; lost in upper motor lesions
Stroke upper inner thigh; lost in upper motor lesions
Extensor Babinski response marks an upper motor lesion

blocks.title: Grading and tips
bullets: Grade 0 absent, plus sluggish or seen only with reinforcement.
Grade double plus is brisk like a normal ankle jerk; triple plus is brisk like a normal knee jerk.
Grade quadruple plus means jerks with clonus; clonus may be brief or sustained.
Boost shy jerks with the Jendrassik grip manoeuvre.
A sole response stays upgoing until 2 years of age.

viva.q: Give the roots of the five limb jerks.
viva.a: Biceps and supinator C5 C6, triceps C6 C7, knee L3 L4, ankle S1.

viva.q: What is the Jendrassik manoeuvre for?
viva.a: Reinforcement that brings out a deep reflex that is otherwise sluggish.

viva.q: Until what age is an upgoing plantar normal?
viva.a: Until 2 years of age.

items.summary: The bedside cluster that marks cerebellar failure: speech, tone, tremor, coordination and walk.

blocks.title: Signs to elicit
bullets: Look for jerky nystagmus on side gaze.
Listen for slow scanning syllabic speech.
Feel for floppy hypotonia and a swinging pendular knee jerk.
Watch for shaking on purpose (intention tremor) and overshoot past the mark (dysmetria).
Test rapid alternate hand flips for dysdiadochokinesia.
Test the rebound phenomenon on sudden release of a held limb.
Do finger nose and knee heel tests for past pointing.
Ask for heel to toe tandem walking and watch for a wide based reeling gait.
Check Romberg stance as part of the balance survey.

viva.q: List five bedside cerebellar signs.
viva.a: Nystagmus, scanning speech, intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesia and a reeling ataxic gait.

viva.q: What is dysmetria?
viva.a: Overshooting or past pointing at the target on finger nose or knee heel testing.

viva.q: How does the cerebellar knee jerk feel?
viva.a: Loose and pendular from the background hypotonia.

items.summary: Neck stiffness and stretch signs of irritated meninges plus a look at skull and spine.

blocks.title: Skull and spine
bullets: Inspect and feel the skull for shape, size, sutures and fontanelle state.
Inspect the whole spine for curve, hair tufts, pits, swellings and tenderness.

blocks.title: Meningeal signs
bullets: Neck rigidity: bending the head forward sets off spasm of the neck extensors.
Kernig sign: with the hip bent, straightening the knee is blocked by painful hamstring spasm.
Brudzinski neck sign: bending the neck folds both hips and knees, best seen sitting.
Brudzinski leg sign: bending one leg folds the opposite hip and knee.
Straight leg raising stretches the same irritated roots and hurts.

blocks.title: Why they occur
bullets: Pull on inflamed spinal roots fires a guarding spasm in the stretched muscles.
A model case pairs suspected TB meningitis with fits, one sided weakness or nerve palsies.
Record raised pressure clues, nutrition grade, growth and vaccine state alongside.

viva.q: How do you elicit Kernig sign?
viva.a: Flex the hip, then try to extend the knee; hamstring spasm blocks it with pain.

viva.q: What is Brudzinski neck sign?
viva.a: Passive neck flexion makes both hips and knees bend, best elicited sitting.

viva.q: Why do meningeal signs arise?
viva.a: Stretching inflamed spinal roots triggers reflex spasm in the pulled muscles.

title.en: Upper versus lower motor neuron weakness

items.summary: A side by side contrast that places a weak limb above or below the anterior horn cell.

head: Feature
Upper motor lesion
Lower motor lesion
rows: Wide and even on both sides
Floppy with little or no tone

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: An upper lesion of the facial nerve leaves the forehead moving.
Fasciculation plus wasting points below the horn cell.
Brisk jerks with an upgoing sole point above it.

viva.q: Give three contrasts of upper versus lower motor lesions.
viva.a: Upper is spastic with brisk jerks and upgoing soles; lower is floppy with wasting and lost jerks.

viva.q: Which lesion shows fasciculation?
viva.a: A lower motor neuron lesion, with marked wasting.

viva.q: What does a spared forehead mean in facial weakness?
viva.a: An upper motor facial lesion above the nucleus.

items.summary: A side by side contrast of the two coordination circuits by power, tone, speech, walk and tremor.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Power stays full in both, so tone, speech and tremor timing tell them apart.
An action tremor is cerebellar; a resting pill rolling tremor is extrapyramidal.

viva.q: How does tone differ between the two?
viva.a: Floppy hypotonia in cerebellar disease, cogwheel rigidity in extrapyramidal disease.

viva.q: How does the tremor differ?
viva.a: Cerebellar tremor strikes on intended action; extrapyramidal tremor rolls at rest.

viva.q: How does the gait differ?
viva.a: Reeling wide based walk in cerebellar disease, shuffling short step walk in extrapyramidal disease.

items.summary: A fifteen point scale that scores eye opening, speech and movement to track consciousness.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Add the three best scores; the total runs from 3 to 15.
Bending to pain is decorticate posture and straightening is decerebrate.

viva.q: What are the three parts of the coma scale?
viva.a: Eye opening out of 4, verbal out of 5 and motor out of 6.

viva.q: What is the lowest and highest total?
viva.a: Lowest 3, highest 15.

viva.q: How do decorticate and decerebrate differ?
viva.a: Decorticate bends the arms to pain; decerebrate straightens them.

items.summary: The ten point checklist that marks a fit with fever as simple and benign.

blocks.title: Criteria
bullets: Age between 6 months and 5 years.
Child was developing normally with no prior nerve disease.
No brain infection is present during the episode.
Fits run in the family.
The fit comes within 24 hours of fever onset.
Only one fit occurs in that illness.
The fit is generalised tonic clonic.
The fit lasts under 10 minutes.
No weakness or deficit follows the fit.
Brain tracing and scan are normal.

blocks.title: Points to remember
bullets: Every point must hold for the simple label; failure of any moves toward complex.
Fever plus brain infection is meningitis workup, never simple febrile fit.

viva.q: What age range defines a simple febrile seizure?
viva.a: From 6 months to 5 years.

viva.q: What time and length limits apply?
viva.a: Within 24 hours of fever, single episode, lasting under 10 minutes.

viva.q: What must follow up show?
viva.a: No deficit after the fit, with normal EEG and normal CT.
